newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: UN envoy tries to build peace out of Congo truce.
newsitem.headline: UN envoy tries to build peace out of Congo truce.

text.p: Rival Congolese militias put down their arms on Wednesday for a 72-hour ceasefire, giving a fillip to peacemakers trying to extinguish a ferocious war that has ravaged the capital Brazzaville.

Mohamed Sahnoun, the special U.N. envoy for central Africa, took advantage of the lull to fly in for meetings with the fighters' leaders -- President Pascal Lissouba and his rival and predecessor, former Marxist Denis Sassou Nguesso.

"It's incredibly quiet, it's amazing," Darcy Christen of the international Red Cross (ICRC) said by telephone from the heart of the city that has been fragmented into opposing camps by fighting since June 5.

Military leaders from both sides agreed on Wednesday to a Red Cross request to open a humanitarian corridor to get help to wounded or stranded people through the front line that cuts the city centre beside the Congo river, officials said.
"We hope to start tomorrow, but maybe that's wishful thinking," said Christen, who said a "burial committee" was also due on Thursday to collect the remains of victims.
Some 200 dead were collected in the early days of the fighting but hundreds more lie where they died in the streets.

The United States, anxious about security once the remnants of a 1,250-strong French army evacuation force in Brazzaville leaves by the weekend, closed its embassy on Wednesday and flew out the ambassador and all diplomats.
As the Americans left, Sahnoun flew in to press ahead with peace talks that stalled on Monday in neighbouring Gabon.

"He will try to overcome some of the obstacles that we encountered...in the talks. The rest of the negotiators are in Libreville awaiting the outcome of Sahnoun's visit," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said in New York on Tuesday.

Lissouba's aides said Sahnoun met the president whose authority has shrunk to a central part of town, and went on to visit Sassou Nguesso, whose 13-year rule ended in free elections five years ago, in his northern suburbs stronghold.
Fighting erupted on June 5 between Lissouba's government forces and "Zulu" militia, and Sassou Nguesso's "Cobras" ahead of presidential elections set for July 27.

The battle for the city of a million people has left hundreds dead and scuppered plans for the poll in which the two men were leading contenders with Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas, who controls a peaceful third section of the city.
Rocket launchers and heavy artillery have been used in the battles for control which have proven as yet inconclusive.
The Red Cross's Christen said his priority was to help an estimated 800 to 1500 untreated wounded.

He said the city centre remained a deserted and looted no man's land but Lissouba aides said that in other areas, some people had ventured out. "People are tired of staying at home. In some areas life has timidly resumed," a spokesman said.
Under the truce accord the city airport should be treated as a neutral zone and be used for humanitarian purposes.
The airport, which the French had been guarding, is a prime target in the city that until recently seemed like a haven of peace while war raged in neighbouring Zaire.
Authorities in the former Zaire capital of Kinshasa, across the mighty Congo river, on Thursday banned people from crossing by canoes to and from Kolelas' peaceful part of Brazzaville.
Sahnoun and other mediators are trying to find at least a temporary solution to stop fighting flaring again at the weekend when the truce is over and the French gone.
Paris has been deaf to Lissouba's entreaties that its troops should stay, either alone or as part of an international force.
Sassou Nguesso, who ran the country from 1979 until 1992, told French radio he was not opposed to an international force.
